title: Clean Your Ducts or Replace Your HVAC System?
h1: Should I Clean My Ducts or Replace My HVAC System?
description: Duct cleaning and HVAC replacement solve different problems. Here is which one fits your symptoms, from dust and odors to uneven rooms and breakdowns.
quick_answer: Clean your ducts when the problem is dust, debris, pet hair or odors in the air while the equipment itself works well. Replace the HVAC system when it is aging, breaking down often, using outdated refrigerant or no longer keeps up. Many homes need neither, or need duct repair, so an inspection should come first.
body:
Homeowners often ask us which of these they need. The short version is that they fix different things. Duct cleaning deals with what's inside the ductwork. Replacement deals with the furnace, air conditioner or heat pump. Sometimes the real fix is a third option, like duct sealing or a simple repair.

What problems does duct cleaning solve?

Duct cleaning removes buildup from the supply and return ducts, registers and sometimes the blower area. It's a good fit when:

  • Dust puffs out of registers when the system starts.
  • You've had a remodel or construction that left drywall dust in the system.
  • Pet hair and dander build up quickly on registers and return grilles.
  • There's evidence of rodents or insects in the ducts.
  • The home has been through heavy wildfire smoke.
  • You've moved into a home and don't know when the ducts were last cleaned.

Cleaning won't fix a weak compressor, a cracked heat exchanger or an undersized system. It also won't fix ducts that are crushed, torn or disconnected. Those need repair.

When does replacing the system make more sense?

Replacement is about the equipment. Signs point that way when:

  • The system is older and needs a major repair, like a compressor, coil or heat exchanger.
  • You're calling for repairs more often.
  • The air conditioner uses R-22 refrigerant and has a leak.
  • Energy bills keep rising without a change in how you use the system.
  • The system can't keep the house comfortable even after repairs and maintenance.

A new system can give you better efficiency, quieter operation and more even temperatures, especially with variable-speed equipment. It won't clean dirty ducts, though, and it won't perform well on ducts that leak.

What if the ducts themselves are the problem?

In many San Diego County homes, ducts run through the attic. Over the years, flexible ducts can sag, get crushed during other work, pull loose at the joints or get damaged by rodents. When that happens, conditioned air leaks into the attic, and the system runs longer to make up for it.

Symptoms of duct problems often look like equipment problems:

  • One or two rooms that never get comfortable.
  • Weak airflow at some registers.
  • Higher bills without an obvious cause.
  • More dust in the house than usual.

In those cases, sealing, repairing or replacing sections of duct can make a bigger difference than either cleaning or new equipment.

Can you do both at the same time?

Yes, and it often makes sense. If you're replacing the system, it's a good time to inspect the ducts. Connecting new equipment to dirty or leaky ducts limits what the new system can do. If the ducts are old, damaged or the wrong size for the new system, replacing them during the installation is usually easier than doing it later.

If the equipment is in good shape and the ducts are dirty, cleaning alone may be all you need.

How do you figure out which one you need?

A good inspection looks at both sides:

  1. The equipment. Age, condition, refrigerant type, repair history and how well it's running.
  2. The ducts. Buildup inside, leaks, crushed or disconnected runs, insulation and sizing.
  3. The house. Attic insulation, air leaks and comfort problems by room.

From there, we explain what we found and what each option would fix. Learn more about our HVAC repair and replacement service and our air duct cleaning and repair service.

What should you avoid?

Be cautious of any recommendation for replacement that comes without a look at the ducts, or for duct cleaning without anyone looking inside them. A camera inspection or a look at a few registers and the return can show whether there's real buildup. And avoid replacing a working system just because the ducts are dirty. Those are two separate problems with two separate fixes.

The same goes the other way. If your furnace or AC is failing, cleaning the ducts won't buy it more years. Spending money on the right fix first, then handling the other item when it actually needs attention, keeps the total cost down and gets you the comfort you were after.
faqs: Will duct cleaning make my HVAC system more efficient?
Cleaning can help if heavy buildup was restricting airflow, but it is not a fix for worn equipment or leaky ducts. Sealing leaks usually has a bigger effect on efficiency than cleaning alone.
Should I clean my ducts before installing a new system?

If the ducts are dirty, yes. Cleaning or replacing them during the installation keeps old dust and debris from circulating through the new equipment. The ducts should also be checked for leaks and sizing.
How do I know if my ducts are leaking?
Common signs include rooms that never get comfortable, weak airflow at some registers, more dust than usual and higher bills. A technician can inspect the attic ducts and test airflow to confirm.
Can dirty ducts make my system break down?
Heavy buildup can restrict airflow, which makes the system work harder. Dirty filters are a more common cause of airflow problems, so start there.
